paper.title: A Provable-Security Treatment of the Key-Wrap Problem (introduces SIV); AES instantiation specified in RFC 5297 'Synthetic Initialization Vector (SIV) Authenticated Encryption Using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)'

program.how: written for ounce-core from the RFC 5297 description (S2V over AES-CMAC, AES-CTR with bits 31 and 63 of the IV cleared) and FIPS 197 AES (S-box computed); no third-party code copied. Encryption direction only. The Rogaway-Shrimpton paper's own text was not fetched
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: RFC 5297 Appendix A.1 (deterministic AEAD, AES-SIV with a 256-bit key, one AD string, 14-byte plaintext) and A.2 (nonce-based, two AD strings plus a nonce, 47-byte plaintext): for each, CMAC(zero), the S2V result (the IV), the CTR start value, the ciphertext and the full IV||C output match (10 of 10 values)

expected_values_source.what: RFC 5297 Appendix A test vectors, parsed mechanically from the fetched RFC text
expected_values_source.note: the vectors are data, copied as numbers

negative_control: built with -DSIV_RB=0x86 (doubling constant 0x86 instead of 0x87), 1 of 10 values matches (CMAC(zero), which does not use the doubled subkeys) and the program exits 1; check.sh reports NOT REPRODUCED
not_checked: SIV's security (nonce-misuse resistance, PRF/PRP security of the construction) or any cryptanalysis
SIV decryption and authentication failure handling; AES-SIV with 384/512-bit keys (RFC 5297 gives only the 256-bit vectors); the later AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452), which is a different construction
inputs other than the two printed vectors (only two vectors exist in the RFC)
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about any hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces exactly the values printed in RFC 5297's two test vectors. It does not show AES-SIV is secure.
